title: Multiscale Quantum-Classical Simulation of Protein Autoproteolysis in a Million-Atom Membrane Environment
authors: Alexander Orlov, Alexis Ralli, Tim Weaving, Michael Williams de la Bastida, Reuben Martin, Zohim Chandani, Minh Chung, P. V. Sriluckshmy, Fedor Simkovic, Luigi Iapichino, Peter J. Love, Christian B. Mendl, Andrea Townsend-Nicholson, Peter V. Coveney
abstract: Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.
summary: This work presents a novel, multiscale quantum-classical simulation framework to study protein autoproteolysis in a massive, membrane-embedded system. By tightly coupling MD, DFT, and quantum wavefunction methods, the authors extend highly accurate electronic structure calculations to biologically relevant scales. This demonstrates a pathway for quantum computers to accelerate simulations of complex chemical reactions in biology.
main_problem: The core challenge is accurately predicting chemical reaction mechanisms in large, complex biomolecular systems where reactive centers are embedded in environments that significantly influence electronic structure.
main_result: The authors successfully applied a hybrid quantum-classical workflow to model the autoproteolysis of a large receptor, showing that correlated electronic structure methods can be extended to biologically relevant scales.
method: A multiscale, hybrid workflow combining Molecular Dynamics, DFT, and correlated wavefunction methods (like QSCI), integrating CPUs, GPUs, and QPUs.
model_or_system: The system is the ADGRG1 adhesion G protein-coupled receptor undergoing autoproteolysis, modeled in a biologically realistic environment exceeding one million atoms within an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane.
key_observables: Reaction barriers, reaction rates, and the specific autoproteolytic cleavage pathway (N–O acyl shift).
important_parameters: The simulation spans multiple length and accuracy scales, incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and thousands of GPU cores.
main_assumptions: The quantum advantage is noted as unproven, and the final WF-in-DFT-in-MD energies are single-point calculations that neglect the full structural relaxation of the environment.

paper_structure: The paper outlines a modular, multi-stage workflow: 1) MD sampling of conformations, 2) QM/MM reaction-path reconstruction via constrained scans, 3) Embedding the active space Hamiltonian, and 4) Treating the active space using quantum computational resources (QPU-assisted diagonalization).
why_interesting: The integration of quantum computing resources (QPU) directly into a chemically demanding, multiscale simulation workflow for biomolecules is highly relevant, pushing the boundaries of simulating open quantum systems in complex chemical environments.
